content.review:
Posterior Sampling: Make Reinforcement Learning Sample Efficient Again
===============================================================

This paper proposes an implementation of PSRL via Neural-PSRL: a neural network is trained fit the transition dynamics, with a last-layer linear approximation used to give a posterior distribution.
This model can be used in conjunction with a policy gradient algorithm to give an exploratory policy.
Evaluated on Mujoco benchmarks this leads to state of the art performance.


There are several things to like about this paper:
- The problem of extending "efficient exploration" to Deep RL is an important one, and PSRL seems like one of the most suitable general approaches to base an algorithm on.
- The proposed algorithm seems reasonable, and seems like it also performs well.
- The approach to writing and accessible code release should be praised.

However, there are some other places where this paper falls down:
- Despite the focus on "incorporating prior knowledge" in the early part of the paper, it seems like the proposed method actually incorporates very little prior knowledge... for example, the "Eluder dimension" of the space represented by these neural networks is presumably huge! This seems like a bit of a bait and switch.
- I don't think the experiments offer a huge amount of *insight* into what is really happening in the algorithm. It would be helpful to show *really good* performance even on a toy domain, so that you can really say that the exploration via PSRL is really working... maybe something like bsuite = https://github.com/deepmind/bsuite and particularly the "deep sea" experiments could help?
- It's a problem that the actual main paper doesn't give a clear and concise description of the algorithm used. I think this is quite important and it would be much better to put the older results on PSRL to the appendix instead.

Minor points:
- I'm not sure the title is a great idea... it might put off some people, but also I don't think it's really warranted from the results... it seems like Neural-PSRL is a potentially interesting avenue, but hardly making anything great (again?)!
- You might want to connect / contrast this work vs the line of research around "Randomized Value Functions" http://jmlr.org/papers/v20/18-339.html... which is another approach that tries to extend something like PSRL to Deep RL.


Overall, I do think this is an interesting paper, and a promising avenue for research.
However there are probably too many places where the paper could be tightened up: clarity of algorithm description, clarity of support/results, separation of actual claims vs claims of "making great" ;D.

display_title: Thank you for the helpful review

content.title: Thank you for the helpful review
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for his / her insightful comments, and are glad to hear that the reviewer also believes that PSRL is at least in theory a promising approach to approach efficient exploration in the Deep RL context and that our proposed algorithm seams reasonable.

Through the reviewer’s well thought out comments it has become clear to us that additional work is required to make the case for our Neural-PSRL algorithm. This includes:

Carefully explaining why our method does indeed incorporate prior knowledge. We failed to highlight the fact that use a highly regularized neural network trained on normalized data. The regularization ensures that only a small subset of weights can have a large value, greatly restricting the Eluder dimension of the space of possible functions. Since we failed to sufficiently explain this detail, it is understandable that the reviewer felt this was a bait-and-switch.
providing insight into what is happening inside the algorithm. It’s still a bit of an open question how best to do this, since there are many moving components (learned prior over MDPs, sampled MDPs, estimated value functions, learned policies…). This may involve formulating a simplified, discrete PSRL method.  While a discrete PSRL applied to “deep sea” or similar environments would be instructive, we’re not sure how novel this contribution would be given the excellent theoretical work that has already been done on PSRL with respect to discrete problems.
As other reviewers have already pointed out, a clear and well motivated description of the method will be in our next submission.

On the subject of randomized value functions: Although both Neural-PSRL and randomized value functions are sampling methods in RL, it’s a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison since our method is a model based method, and randomized value functions is a model free method.

content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review:
The authors implement Thompson sampling for finite horizon MDPs in a continuous control setting where they learn the uncertainty over the dynamics using a Bayesian linear regression model on top of a neural network embedding. They use model-based RL to learn the optimal policy for a sample from the posterior. Specifically, they use a variant of SAC on unrolls from the learned model. The optimization is not entirely clear from Algorithm 2--it seems that they backpropagate through the learned model and a ground truth reward function. This is very reminiscent of Stochastic Value Gradients (Heess, 2015) yet they do not cite this paper. Important ingredient to make the model based RL to work is to use an ensemble of policies. The work lacks in theoretical novelty since the Thompson sampling approach is established and well-known. This would be perfectly fine if the experiments demonstrated clear improvements but that is not the case.

1. The paper is too wordy and repetitive--there's no reason to spend 5 pages discussing Thompson sampling and the motivations of Bayesian RL.
2. As also pointed out by the authors it is not clear if the observed improvements are not due to the ensemble of policies. This seems like it should be easy to check by running the other methods with ensembles of policies too.
3. More generally, since the hypothesis of the paper is that incorporating the uncertainty is important, the experiments should focus on that, and e.g. validate that the proposed approach to learning the posterior actually learns the correct uncertainty. One possible ablation would be to simply add (annealed) noise to the weights and check if maybe such an unstructured distribution over dynamics would work too.

display_title: We thank the reviewer for the comment, address the reviewer's suggestion

content.title: We thank the reviewer for the comment, address the reviewer's suggestion
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for his / her comments on our paper, and we believe his / her thoughts will help us formulate a clearer and more profound paper in the future.

The reference to Stochastic Value Gradients (Heess, 2015) is indeed very helpful. We regret failing to cite this important work, after reading their paper we wholeheartedly concur that elements of Algorithm 2 are reminiscent of their work.

We thank the reviewer for his / her suggestion and agree that other methods could potentially be improved by the ensemble of policies, and plan to investigate this further.

The suggestion that we “validate that the proposed approach to learning the posterior actually learns the correct uncertainty,” is not a sensible or possible goal. The posterior over possible MDPs which we discuss in our paper models the epistemic uncertainty in the system (i.e. the uncertainty we have about the underlying dynamics of a system, vs. aleatoric uncertainty, the uncertainty created by random fluctuations within the system which can be modeled by a sufficiently powerful statistical model). While it is easy to verify if a model captures Aleatoric uncertainty (i.e. the observed distribution of errors matches the modeled distribution of errors), verifying that a model captures the epistemic uncertainty is much more difficult and requires knowledge of the prior from which the underlying MDP was sampled. For different priors, different models of the posterior will work better or worse. Therefore the choice of method to model the posterior amounts to an educated guess. and we elected to use the NeuralLinear model due to its simplicity and show that this method works on benchmark RL problems, without claiming that other priors over MDPs (e.g. networks with annealed noise over the weights) will perform better or worse.

By demonstrating the effectiveness of Neural-PSRL with the Neural Linear model as a prior, we demonstrate the effectiveness of Neural-PSRL in general and leave it as an open question for future research which priors are most effective for which classes of problems.

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I did not assess the derivations or theory.
content.review:
The paper suggests a practical implementation of Posterior Sampling for Reinforcement Learning (PSLR) using deep networks. The PSLR framework assumes that the model of the environment is sampled from a relatively lower dimensional distribution (for example because of some inherent structure they posses), and exploits this to reduce the sampling complexity to learn an optimal policy, so that the number of samples required is bounded by the complexity of the model distribution, and not by the dimensionality of the state or action space.

The paper is well motivated and well written, and the research direction is indeed interesting. I would like to see the implementation section pushing further the limits of the theory by using a more complex posterior model – rather than a simple linear layer – and by testing on more challenging environments, where explicitly exploiting the structure of the non-linear model is essential to solve the task.

Regarding the implementation, in Section 4.2 the model is parametrized as s' = W z + s, where W is sampled from the posterior and z is the output of a feed-forward network. Could you further comment on which data the feed-forward network is trained on? Does the theoretical framework remain valid if the feed-forward network is trained only on states from the environment on which the PSLR will later be tested? Wouldn't that imply that the prior model distribution is already biased toward the particular environment?

display_title: We thank the reviewer for their comments and insightful questions and attempt to answer the question

content.title: We thank the reviewer for their comments and insightful questions and attempt to answer the question
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for his / her helpful comments. We very much agree that testing on more challenging environments would greatly help demonstrate the effectiveness of this method, and we are currently working on this. As far as testing “more complex posterior model – rather than a simple linear layer,” while this is possible it is currently our sentiment, and we have come to believe the sentiment of the other reviewers that we should first more carefully motivate and explain the existing method while further investigating, generating insights into and demonstrating the effectiveness via empirical studies of our method before exploring more advanced variants thereof. The current posterior model isn’t simply as linear layer

Regarding the reviewer’s question, we thank the reviewer for the insightful question and regret that our draft did not explain this important detail carefully enough. The feed forward neural network in question is trained on all past state-action-next state triplets, meaning for every past environment interaction, the state-action pair is fed into the bottom of the network, and the network is trained to predict the difference between the previous and next states. It is the last hidden layer of this network which is the z which is used as an input to the s' = W z + s next-state prediction model, where W is selected using bayesian linear regression.

It is our understanding that the review’s question raises two questions: 1) is the choice of prior (feed forward neural network with Bayesian linear regression layer) already biased toward the particular environment? And 2) What are the theoretical implications after some environment interactions have been observed and the prior has been updated with these interactions (giving us a posterior distribution over environments)?

On the first question, the answer is a resounding yes. This choice of prior above (feed forward network plus sampled last layer) assumes the true environment is such that the next state us the result of a deterministic continuous function conditioned only on the previous state and the action. A counterexample would be an environment where the next state is the result of a deterministic function plus noise. There, no environment sampled from the prior proposed above would be close to the true environment (all sampled environments would be deterministic, while the true environment is stochastic). A more complex model prior would be required, a prior over distributions instead of a prior over functions.

This is a key point of our work: If we pick a prior which can model every needle in every haystack, i.e. model the most outlandish distributions then we will indeed be able to model the most outlandish distributions but will also require a lot of samples to learn this distribution. On the other hand, if we pick a prior which is “biased towards the particular environment” (by for example assuming the environment is deterministic and can be modeled by a regularized neural network, or the next state of an environment is equal to some deterministic function plus sub-gaussian noise, thereby biasing us away from outlandish distributions) we will be much more sample efficient assuming our assumptions are correct.

On the second question, it’s a clear yes and no. First the yes: Assume that f:S \times A\to S describes the true transition dynamics of our environment, and z:S\times A\to\mathbb R^n is the last hidden layer of the trained feed-forward neural network conditioned on a state-action pair. Further, assume that there exists a state action pair s,a\in S\times A such that min_{W\in\mathbb R^{n\times m}} || W z(s,a) + s - f(s, a) || is large. Note that it is irrelevant whether that this s, a , f(s,a) state-action-observation triplet has already been observed or not. This means that, due to some unlucky circumstances no accurate model of the true environment can be sampled from our posterior. In this case, the theoretical framework no longer remains valid.

On the no front (and we present this as a conjecture without rigorous proof), this set of unlucky circumstances described above is unlikely to occur for sufficiently wide networks since z(s,a) forms a set of basis functions, meaning that <w_i, z( \cdot, \cdot )> (i.e. the inner product between the hidden layer and the i-th row of the weight matrix) forms a linear combination of such basis functions. Similar to Weierstrass approximation theorem, we can expect there to be a weight vector w_i which reasonably approximates the true dynamics f(s, a).

We again thank the reviewer for his / her comments and hope we have addressed the reviewer's question.

content.title: Official Blind Review #4
content.review:
The authors, in this paper, study the problem of efficient exploration and exploitation in RL. They propose an algorithm, as referred to as a suite of solutions, based on the posterior sampling approach to tackle mainly continuous state-action space MDPs. Their method learns the model of the environment using deep neural networks while having the last layer trained using Bayesian linear regression. They utilize this model to design a policy for the exploration and exploitation trade-off.


A few comments that did not affect my evaluation but might be helpful to the authors: I might suggest to the authors to reconsider the title of their paper. I can guess the authors mean they aim to design a more sample efficient algorithm and by RL in the title, they mean the RL algorithms. Please rephrase it. Also, the term "again" implies that the methods in this filed were sample efficient, then became sample inefficient, and then this paper proposes to make them sample efficient. 

Minor changes: In the middle of page 3, the authors define V_{mu,i}^M. I might have mistaken, but either "i" goes from 1 to tau-1 or V_{mu,tau+1}^M is zero instead of V_{mu,tau}^M to have general MDP setting. Please correct me if I am wrong. 

Also, the sentence on the very same page, "for every previous step the expected future value is the reward at the current step plus all future rewards." might require a bit more attention. I might guess the authors mean the expected reward.... is the value. 

In theorem 1, borrowed from Osband & Van Roy 2014a, I think the term sigma_P is not defined. Also please reconsider calling sigma_R the variance, since in that case, the theorem might not hold. 

Generally, I have a major concern about the presentation of this paper. While the authors spent the first 4 pages on the discussions that are useful, important, and provide intuition, I have a hard time to see the significance and importance of presenting them. Especially, when the authors spent a considerably small portion of their paper on their own contribution and provided very shallow representing of their algorithm. 

Regarding the references, I found this paper not satisfyingly covering the space of literature. Besides the issue of coverage, there are quite a few parts that require citation, but no citation is provided. I would be happy to see a citation related to AdamW, citations of the line of work by Ronald Ortner on continuous MDPs, and also literature on Thompson sampling in linear MDPs. I can extend this list if the authors are interested. 


Regarding the presentation of their method, first of all, I strongly recommend the authors to provide a self-contained, detailed and profound description of their contribution and their algorithm. I also strongly suggest the authors discuss the motivation and then the detail of each component used in their approach. 

I appreciate the fact that the authors provided the code used in their paper, but it would be more appreciated if they would have provided more details of their algorithm, in the paper, to the point that the algorithm could be reproduced by a reader to some extent, without the code.

In order to draw a conclusion on the performance of the proposed method, I would be happy to see a set of significantly more empirical studies. 


Generally, I like the approach and appreciate the authors' effort. While I think the current paper has undoubtedly high potential to improve, I do not think the current version is ready to be published in this conference.

display_title: We thank the reviewer and concur with his / her assessment

content.title: We thank the reviewer and concur with his / her assessment
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for his / her detailed review and find the comments are very helpful in refining our draft for re-submission at a later date. We are especially pleased that the reviewer likes the approach, as we also strongly believe this approach holds much promise. We concur that there is potential to improve, and thank the reviewer for helping us in this improvement process.

On the minor issues, we thank the reviewer for pointing out minor mistakes. As with other reviewers, the reviewer has expressed his / her desire that we devote more space in our paper to a clearer and fuller representation of our algorithm. Further, the reviewer has, as have other reviewers, expressed a desire for significantly more empirical studies. We fully concur with the reviewer on both these points and will be sure to include both these elements in future drafts.

We especially thank the reviewer for the suggested further citations, we will be sure to include these in the future. We regret not citing amung other works AdamW. Further citation suggestions are always welcome, we look eagerly await the reviewer’s further suggestions.

On the connection to randomized value functions, the same issue was raised by reviewer #1, please see our response there.

Since we broadly concur with the reviewer's assessment and there are no open questions, we will keep our reply sort, regret many reviewers found the draft to be lacking and will work to make it a better work. Again we thank the reviewer for his / her comments.
